beads.title: Centralize SQLite-timestamp epoch-ms parsing (core + fleet copies)
beads.locations: src/core/lid-resolver.ts:86 (timestampToEpochMs), src/fleet/health-poller.ts:1196 (readTimestampMs), canonical helper at src/fleet/time-utils.ts:34 (normalizeTimestamp)

beads.title: Consolidate WhatsApp-JID redaction regex (5 divergent copies)

Read-only — do NOT apply.

beads.title: Consolidate credential-redaction regexes + replace chain (bot-errors-outbox vs auth-cli-redaction)
beads.locations: src/lib/bot-errors-outbox.ts:68-107 (SECRETISH_ASSIGNMENT/AUTHORIZATION_BEARER/BEARER_VALUE/WHATSAPP_JID/URL_USERINFO/CREDENTIAL_PATH + redactText replace chain); src/transport/auth-cli-redaction.ts:1-20 (same-named constants + redactAuthCliText replace chain)
beads.risk: Redaction is security-load-bearing; merging keyword lists/regex variants could change what gets masked (broader masking is safe; narrower is not). Must verify both modules' test suites and that the union regex does not regress the ReDoS hardening.
beads.evidence: Both modules define a private set of identically-named secret-redaction constants (SECRETISH_ASSIGNMENT, AUTHORIZATION_BEARER, BEARER_VALUE, WHATSAPP_JID, URL_USERINFO, CREDENTIAL_PATH) and apply the same .replace() pipeline in the same order. Two redaction SSOTs means a security fix to one silently misses the other — exactly the divergence already present.
beads.proposed_action: Extract the shared secret/JID/URL/credential-path patterns and the replace pipeline into one library module (e.g. src/lib/credential-redaction.ts), take the union of keyword lists and the hardened (linear) regex variants, and have both bot-errors-outbox.redactText and auth-cli-redaction.redactAuthCliText consume it. Keep bot-errors-outbox's extra phone-redaction layer as a composed step. Re-run the existing redaction tests for both modules.

beads.title: Extract shared managed-loop API provider scaffold (anthropic-api / openai-api)
beads.risk: These providers are user-facing fallback paths with characterization tests; a base-class refactor must preserve exact event ordering, the active-flag mid-loop break semantics, and the exact friendly-message strings (tests assert them). Behavior-preserving but broad surface.

beads.proposed_action: Hoist the shared pieces into a common module (e.g. a managed-loop base class / helper functions, or extend providers/mcp-bridge.ts): the two constants, the friendly-error string table + status-to-message mapper, the connection-error/self-heal/429-retry callApi prelude, and the sendTurn tool-loop skeleton. beads.title: Collapse 4 inline request-body parsers in health.ts onto readBody()
beads.locations: src/core/health.ts:480-526 (/send), :543-562 (/agent/compact), :712-732 (/access), :804-824 (/mark-read); helper already used at src/core/health.ts:628 via readBody() from src/lib/http.ts:5-30

beads.title: Factor the duplicated keyring backend-lookup blocks in lookupCredential
beads.risk: Keyring is credential-path code; the warn-on-primary-only semantics and the duplicated try/catch fallback ordering must be preserved exactly or a transient backend error could change fallback behavior. Needs both-backend test coverage to confirm equivalence.
beads.evidence: The secret-tool and macos-keychain branches of lookupCredential are structurally identical: each iterates `services.entries()`, runs execFileSync per candidate, warns only on the primary (index===0) candidate failure with the same log message 'keyring read failed — falling back to env lookup', then on the outer path falls back to fileStoreRead(service) and lookupEnvAfterKeyringMiss() — and repeats the same fileStoreRead+lookupEnvAfterKeyringMiss pair again in the catch. The two blocks differ only in how the execFileSync command/args/account are built. ~30 lines of near-identical control flow are maintained twice.
beads.proposed_action: Extract a helper like tryKeyringCandidates(services, runOne: (candidate, isPrimary) => string|null) that owns the candidate loop, primary-only warn, and the fileStoreRead→env fallback tail, then have both branches supply only their execFileSync closure (secret-tool args vs security args+account). Keep the env-only tail as the shared default. Re-run keyring lookup tests for both backends.

beads.title: Fold avatarColor into avatarHueIndex (duplicate hash idiom)
beads.risk: avatarHueIndex accepts string|number|null and normalizes via textValue(); avatarColor takes a plain string jid. Inputs are JID strings so behavior is identical, but confirm no caller relied on avatarColor coercing a non-string. HUE_COUNT=8 must match in both (it does).
beads.evidence: avatarColor() in groups-utils re-implements the exact deterministic 8-hue hash byte-for-byte from avatarHueIndex(): `for (...) hash = ((hash << 5) - hash + char.charCodeAt(i)) | 0; idx = ((hash % 8) + 8) % 8`, then wraps it as `var(--avatar-hue-${idx})`. text-utils.ts:29 even documents that avatarHueIndex uses the 'Same hashing idiom as line-detail/groups-utils.avatarColor'. Avatar.tsx:92 already composes the same string from avatarHueIndex: `var(--avatar-hue-${avatarHueIndex(name)})`. So there are TWO copies of the hash and TWO copies of the token-string template across three files.
beads.proposed_action: Reduce avatarColor to a one-liner over the existing util: `return \`var(--avatar-hue-${avatarHueIndex(jid)})\``, deleting the inline hash loop. Optionally export a shared `avatarHueToken(name)` from text-utils and have both groups-utils and Avatar.tsx call it, so the `var(--avatar-hue-N)` template lives in one place too.

rejected.title: Repeated SQL WHERE-clause builders across substrate list functions
rejected.locations: listBeads beads.ts:103-116, listTriggers triggers.ts:164-172, listEntities entities.ts:218-229
rejected.risk: Low — pure read-path refactor. Each list has slightly different null-handling (`!= null` vs truthy for ownerJid/kind); preserve those exact guards or you change which empty values filter.
rejected.evidence: All three build a dynamic filter the same way: `const w: string[] = []; const b: SQLInputValue[] = []; if (f.x) { w.push('x = ?'); b.push(f.x); } ...; const sql = \`... ${w.length ? 'WHERE ' + w.join(' AND ') : ''} ...\`; return db.prepare(sql).all(...b)`. The clause-accumulator pattern (push predicate + bind in lockstep, then join with ' AND ') is copy-pasted three times with only the column set differing.
rejected.proposed_action: Extract a tiny shared filter builder (e.g. buildWhere(conditions: Array<[predicate, value]>) -> { clause, binds }) in substrate and have all three list functions feed it their column/value pairs. Keep ORDER BY/LIMIT per-callsite since those differ.
rejected.why: Confirmed all three citations exactly. beads.ts:103-116 listBeads, triggers.ts:164-172 listTriggers, entities.ts:218-229 listEntities all use the identical pattern: `const w: string[] = []; const b: SQLInputValue[] = []; if (f.x) { w.push('x = ?'); b.push(f.x); } ...; const sql = `... ${w.length ? 'WHERE ' + w.join(' AND ') : ''} ...`; return db.prepare(sql).all(...b)`. grep confirms no existing buildWhere helper in src/core/substrate/. The clause-accumulator core (push predicate + bind in lockstep, join ' AND ') is genuinely copy-pasted three times. However there are real divergences: listEntities starts with a mandatory `merged_into_id IS NULL` predicate so its WHERE is unconditional (no `w.length ?` ternary), and it includes a LIKE predicate with value transformation (`%${textMatch.toLowerCase()}%`); listTriggers has ORDER BY only (no LIMIT) while the others append LIMIT ?. The duplication is real but small (~3-6 plumbing lines each) and trivial; a shared buildWhere would only absorb the accumulator core while each callsite keeps its own SQL assembly, conditional-WHERE logic, and tail clauses.

rejected.title: Two near-identical merged-entity chain walks in entities.ts
rejected.locations: resolveEntityRef merged_into_id walk at src/core/substrate/entities.ts:86-94; collectMergedIds at :171-186
rejected.risk: These guards protect against corrupt cycles; changing a depth bound could alter which entity wins resolution on malformed data. Keep semantics, only de-magic the constants.
rejected.evidence: Both traverse the entity merge graph with a visited Set and a fixed depth bound (resolveEntityRef: `while (row.merged_into_id != null && visited.size < 10)` following winner-ward; collectMergedIds: `for (let depth = 0; depth < 5; depth++)` collecting losers-ward via merged_into_id IN (...)). They walk opposite directions of the same merged_into_id relation with the same cycle-guard intent and divergent depth limits (10 vs 5), which is an easy place for the two bounds to drift out of agreement.
rejected.proposed_action: Document/centralize the merge-graph traversal: at minimum share a single MAX_MERGE_DEPTH constant between the two walks so the winner-ward and losers-ward bounds stay consistent; optionally factor the cycle-safe step into a small helper. Direction differs so full unification is not required.
rejected.why: Both cited walks exist exactly as described: resolveEntityRef at entities.ts:86-94 has `while (row.merged_into_id != null && visited.size < 10)` (winner-ward), and collectMergedIds at :171-186 has `for (let depth = 0; depth < 5; depth++)` collecting losers-ward via `merged_into_id IN (...)`. But the "near-identical duplication" framing does not hold. They are structurally and semantically different traversals of the same relation: (1) resolveEntityRef is a single-pointer linked-list chase — one hop per iteration following row.merged_into_id, with `visited` used purely as a cycle guard, and the bound counts chain HOPS; (2) collectMergedIds is a breadth-first fan-IN expansion — each iteration set-expands all entities pointing at the current frontier, the Set accumulates the RESULT (not just cycle-guard), and it has its own natural `if (!added) break` termination; the bound counts BFS LEVELS. The two numeric limits (10 vs 5) measure different quantities (chain length vs fan-in depth), so they are NOT expected to be equal and a shared MAX_MERGE_DEPTH would be semantically wrong/misleading, not a safety improvement. Full unification is impossible (the reviewer concedes this), and even the minimal proposed action (share a constant) conflates two distinct dimensions. mergeEntities (:142-149) already forbids merging into an already-merged entity, so deep chains/cycles are defensive belt-and-suspenders, not a live drift risk.

The only truly common kernel is ~3-4 lines. A parsePinoBase returning {obj,level,label,timestamp,msg,component} can't serve both cleanly (label semantics differ, msg/component extraction differs, empty-msg handling differs), so net dedup is marginal.

rejected.title: Reuse the cooldown throttle for the auth in-flight/timeout machinery or document the divergence
rejected.locations: src/fleet/routes/credentials.ts:82-110 (MUTATION_COOLDOWN_MS + throttle + mutationLastCall, reused for VERIFY_COOLDOWN_MS), src/fleet/routes/ops.ts:1236-1242 (activeAuthProcesses/authInFlight/AUTH_TIMEOUT_MS)
rejected.risk: Medium — auth flow has SSE teardown, child-process kill, and instance-restore concerns that a generic cooldown does not model; do not force-fit. Lowest-priority item.
rejected.evidence: credentials.ts already generalized a per-service throttle (`throttle(res, store, cooldownMs, service, label)`) reused by both the mutation (1s) and verify (10s) cooldowns. ops.ts handleAuth maintains its own ad-hoc per-instance concurrency guards (authInFlight Set + activeAuthProcesses Map + AUTH_TIMEOUT_MS) with hand-rolled add/delete around the SSE lifecycle. These are not identical mechanisms but both are 'one in-flight operation per key + bounded duration' guards solved twice.
rejected.proposed_action: Evaluate whether handleAuth's single-flight guard can reuse a shared keyed-lock/throttle primitive (the credentials throttle is the closest existing one). If the SSE long-lived semantics make sharing impractical, leave as-is — this is the weakest finding; only consolidate if a third single-flight guard appears.
rejected.why: The two mechanisms exist as cited but are not the same logic. credentials.ts throttle (credentials.ts:95-110) is a time-based RATE LIMIT: Map<string,number> of last-call timestamps that is NEVER released on completion; a later call compares elapsed time and returns 429. It is consumed by the 1s mutation cooldown (lines 152, 221) and the 10s verify cooldown (line 258). ops.ts handleAuth (ops.ts:1236-1390) implements a SINGLE-FLIGHT LOCK plus a process registry plus a watchdog: authInFlight (Set<string>) is acquired on entry (line 1260) and explicitly RELEASED on completion in the createSSEWriter cleanup callback (line 1307), returning 409 on contention; activeAuthProcesses (Map<string,ChildProcess>) stores live child handles to SIGTERM a prior session (lines 1263-1267, 1299, 1306); AUTH_TIMEOUT_MS drives a per-stream setTimeout watchdog (line 1320-1325) that kills the child, restores the stopped instance, and ends the SSE stream. These differ in release model (never-released elapsed-time vs acquire/release lock), stored payload (timestamp vs ChildProcess handle), response code (429 vs 409), and the presence of a side-effecting timer. The throttle primitive cannot express the lock's acquire-on-entry/release-on-completion semantics without imposing a spurious post-success cooldown, and would not eliminate the separate process-registry Map or the watchdog. The only commonality is 'a string-keyed collection,' which is too generic to be a real clone. The reviewer's own evidence admits 'these are not identical mechanisms' and the proposed action is to leave as-is unless a third guard appears (it has not).

These are generic record-traversal primitives, not migration-specific, yet they live privately in this one module. getPath/hasPath are near-identical (hasPath is getPath returning a boolean), and the codebase already centralizes the isRecord guard they all build on in src/lib/type-guards.ts — signaling these traversal helpers are the kind of thing meant to be shared rather than re-implemented per consumer.

Keep cloneJson local unless a shared deep-clone already exists. Behavior-preserving; covered by migration tests.
rejected.why: The cited helpers exist exactly at src/config-memory-migration.ts:52-106 (cloneJson, getPath, hasPath, ensureRecordPath, setPath, deletePath), and getPath/hasPath ARE near-identical traversal loops differing only in return type. So the literal observation holds. However the finding's central thrust — these are generic primitives meant to be shared/promoted to src/lib — does not hold up: grep across src/ and tests/ shows ZERO other modules re-implementing dotted-path get/set/has/delete. Every other `split('.')` site is domain-specific (baileys-version, IP octets in links.ts, cron fields, JWT in auth-ticket.ts) — none is a record-path toolkit. There is no existing shared object-path util or deep-clone in src/lib (cloneJson and the path helpers are the only matches repo-wide). The proposal's fallback ('collapse hasPath into getPath(...) !== undefined') is also imperfect: hasPath uses `part in current`, so a stored literal `undefined` would diverge from getPath — only safe here because values are JSON-loaded. Net: real overlap, but a single-consumer pair of ~7-line private helpers with a subtle in-vs-undefined semantic and no sharing opportunity.

rejected.title: Inline pad/date-key helpers re-derive calendar-utils' dayKey
rejected.locations: DateTimePicker.tsx:129 (`const pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(2,'0')`); ScheduleComposerModal.tsx:70 (same pad); calendar-utils.ts:84-89 (dayKey) and :171-177 (setDateOnly build YYYY-MM-DD)
rejected.risk: Low; pad2 is pure. Verify the composer/picker aren't constructing strings in a subtly different order than dayKey before swapping to the higher-level helpers (the pad2 swap alone is risk-free).
rejected.evidence: DateTimePicker and ScheduleComposerModal each define a local `pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(2,'0')` to assemble datetime-local strings, while calendar-utils.ts already owns dayKey() (YYYY-MM-DD) and setDateOnly() doing the same zero-pad date assembly. The two-digit zero-pad idiom recurs across calendar-utils (4x), DateTimePicker, ScheduleComposerModal, and scheduled-utils:59.
rejected.proposed_action: Export a small `pad2(n)` from calendar-utils (or reuse dayKey/setDateOnly where a full date string is being built) and import it in DateTimePicker and ScheduleComposerModal instead of re-declaring the closure.
rejected.why: Verified all cited lines. DateTimePicker.tsx:129 and ScheduleComposerModal.tsx:70 each genuinely declare `const pad = (n: number) => String(n).padStart(2, '0')` (confirmed verbatim), and both build a full datetime-local string `${y}-${pad(m+1)}-${pad(d)}T${pad(h)}:${pad(min)}` (DateTimePicker:131-132, ScheduleComposerModal:72-73). calendar-utils.ts uses the same padStart(2,'0') idiom inline 4x (ymKey:45, dayKey:86-87, setDateOnly:175-176). scheduled-utils.ts:59 uses it too, plus MessageContent.tsx (106,151) the reviewer missed. So the literal pad2 idiom is genuinely repeated and a `pad2(n)` export would consolidate the two closure declarations — the duplication EXISTS. BUT the reviewer's framing overstates the reuse target: dayKey() produces date-only YYYY-MM-DD (no time) and setDateOnly() preserves/defaults time from a source string via regex — neither is a drop-in for "format a fresh Date as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm", so the proposed "reuse dayKey/setDateOnly" path would lose meaning. Only the narrow pad2 extraction is valid, and that consolidates a 1-line zero-pad closure across two files in different dirs (primitives/ vs line-detail/), adding a cross-module import where ScheduleComposerModal currently imports nothing from calendar-utils.
